keyVerseText: There were also women looking on afar off: among whom was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome;
rootMeaning: The name Σαλώμη (Salome) is derived from the Hebrew root שָׁלוֹם (shâlôwm), which conveys a rich range of meanings centered on peace, completeness, welfare, and well-being. This root implies not only the absence of conflict but also a state of holistic prosperity and safety. Thus, the name Salome carries the connotation of one who embodies or is associated with peace and wholeness, which goes beyond a simple personal identifier to suggest a spiritual and communal blessing.
usageInScripture: The word Σαλώμη appears twice in the New Testament, both times transliterated as Salome, referring to an Israelitess. Its consistent translation as a proper name indicates its function as a personal identifier rather than a descriptive term. The occurrences in Mark 15:40 and 16:1 situate Salome within the group of women followers of Jesus, highlighting her role in the Gospel narrative. This limited but focused usage underscores her identity as a faithful witness.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Salome’s name as rooted in the concept of peace enriches our appreciation of her presence in the Gospel accounts. The peace implied in her name reflects the deeper peace Christ brings to believers, a peace that transcends circumstances and embodies spiritual wholeness. As a follower of Jesus who stood near the cross and witnessed the resurrection events, Salome personifies the peace and hope that come through faith in Christ’s redemptive work. Her name reminds Christians that the gospel is not only about salvation from sin but also about entering into the fullness of God’s peace.
keyVerseReflection: Mark 15:40 notes that Salome was among the women observing Jesus from a distance during His crucifixion, alongside Mary Magdalene and others. The mention of Salome here emphasizes her faithful presence at a critical moment in salvation history. Her name, meaning peace, poignantly contrasts with the turmoil of the crucifixion scene, reminding readers that even in suffering and apparent defeat, God's peace remains accessible to those who trust in Him.
